editions.text:
September 17 added up to one of the busiest days of the week, with 302 feeder visits and 21 species recorded against a seven-day average of roughly 170 visits. Tufted Titmice remained the dominant feeder presence, accounting for 123 of the visits, while Carolina Chickadees and Ruby-throated Hummingbirds also held steady as regulars.

The acoustic record was dominated by Carolina Wrens, which contributed 132 detections, and Northern Cardinals, with 39. Several other species, including Blue Jays and Gray Catbirds, were heard frequently, while rare visitors like the Red-shouldered Hawk and White-eyed Vireo appeared briefly. All ten species that appear daily at this station were recorded again.

Activity at the station shifted following the installation of a new seed feeder earlier in the week, which replaced a unit previously causing detection problems. This change aligns with the rise in visual records, where Tufted Titmice and Carolina Chickadees filled the majority of visits.

The morning opened with a chorus before the light fully took hold, led by Carolina Wrens whose detections began at 06:00 and peaked significantly by 08:00. While the air filled with the calls of Northern Cardinals and American Crows, the feeder itself remained largely quiet until the mid-morning. By 10:14, the first probable visual sighting appeared, a Tufted Titmouse that initiated a short, sharp burst of activity lasting only fourteen minutes.

Today’s total of six feeder visits is far below the 130-visit norm for this time of day. The few confirmed sightings were dominated by Tufted Titmice and a couple of Carolina Chickadees, while the broader acoustic landscape included fleeting notes of Blue Jays and a distant Red-shouldered Hawk. Despite the heavy vocal presence of species like Eastern Towhees and Northern Mockingbirds, the physical traffic at the station has remained subdued.

The last confident visual record was from 08:28.

Tufted Titmice and House Finches drive most visits through the early afternoon. A Tufted Titmouse arrives at 10:14. A White-breasted Nuthatch visits at 11:14. By 15:30, the total stands at 40 visits, below the recent seven-day average of over 160.

The afternoon air is warm and still, with a high of 28.9°C and wind only 3 kph. Northern Cardinals are more vocal in the last two hours. Ruby-throated Hummingbirds make two confident visits, the last at 12:58. Eastern Phoebes are seen twice in probable sightings around 13:00.

House Finches account for the majority of the confirmed visual visits.

The day closed with 99 feeder visits, a significant drop from the recent seven-day average of nearly 200. While the afternoon saw a surge of House Finches and Tufted Titmice, the overall traffic remained subdued compared to the 300-plus visits recorded yesterday. The station registered the full breadth of local species, with 17 kinds confirmed through both sound and sight, though the physical presence at the feeders was sparse.

Acoustically, the day was led by the consistent chorus of Carolina Wrens and the persistent calls of Northern Cardinals. A Red-shouldered Hawk was detected 16 times, its presence noted distinctly in the late afternoon hours.

Dusk arrived with a final, brief visit from a Ruby-throated Hummingbird at 19:40, just six minutes after sunset. Before that, a cluster of Carolina Chickadees and Tufted Titmice moved through the feeders in the 17:00 hour.
